content: Sea-buckthorn, scientifically known as Hippophae L., is a deciduous shrub belonging to the family Elaeagnaceae. The name sea-buckthorn is hyphenated to distinguish it from the unrelated buckthorns of the genus Rhamnus in the family Rhamnaceae. It is also commonly referred to as sea buckthorn, seabuckthorn, sandthorn, or seaberry. Since 2005, there has been increasing recognition of sea-buckthorn berries in the United States, other developed nations, and the global functional food industry due to their exceptional nutrient profile, antioxidant properties, and potential as a novel superfruit. Description and Distribution Sea-buckthorn comprises six species and twelve subspecies, native to a vast region spanning Europe and Asia, including countries such as China, Mongolia, India, Nepal, Pakistan, Russia, Great Britain, France, Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, Poland, Finland, Sweden, and Norway. Approximately 90% of the global sea-buckthorn resources, covering about 1.5 million hectares, are found in China, where the plant is extensively used for soil and water conservation. The shrubs typically grow to heights of 0.5–6 meters, though they can occasionally reach up to 18 meters in Central Asia. They thrive in dry, sandy environments, are tolerant of saline air and soil, and require full sunlight for optimal growth. They do not tolerate shade from larger trees. The most widespread species, Hippophae rhamnoides (common sea-buckthorn), has a range extending from the Atlantic coasts of Europe to northwestern China. In Western Europe, it is primarily found along coastal areas where salt spray inhibits competition from larger plants. In Central Asia, it is more common in arid, semi-desert regions, while in Central Europe and Asia, it can also be found as a subalpine shrub above the tree line in mountainous areas or along sunny riverbanks. The common sea-buckthorn has dense, stiff, and thorny branches. The plant is dioecious, meaning male and female flowers are borne on separate plants. Male flowers are brownish and produce wind-dispersed pollen. Names in Different Languages Sea-buckthorn is known by various names in different languages, such as Чацаргана (Mongolian), Shaji (Chinese), Astelpaju (Estonian), Duindoorn (Dutch), Tyrni (Finnish), Argousier (French), Sanddorn (German), Olivello Spinoso (Italian), Облепиха (Oblepikha, Russian), Espino de Mar/Falso Espino/Espino Amarillo (Spanish), and Havtorn (Swedish and Danish). Berries and Leaves Female sea-buckthorn plants produce orange berries that are 6–9 mm in diameter, soft, juicy, and exceptionally rich in vitamin C, with concentrations averaging 600 mg per 100 grams and sometimes reaching up to 1500 mg per 100 grams. Some varieties are also abundant in vitamin A, vitamin E, and oils. These berries serve as an essential winter food source for certain bird species, such as fieldfares. The leaves are consumed by the larvae of various Lepidoptera species, including the coastal race of the Ash Pug moth, Brown-tail, The Dun-bar, Emperor Moth, Mottled Umber, and Coleophora elaeagnisella. The species Hippophae salicifolia (Willow-leaved Sea-buckthorn) is native to the Himalayas, growing at high altitudes in dry valleys south of the range of H. rhamnoides. It is characterized by broader (up to 10 mm wide), greener (less silvery) leaves and yellow berries. A wild variant of this species grows at even higher altitudes in the alpine zone, forming low shrubs no taller than 1 meter with small leaves measuring 1–3 cm in length. Uses Harvesting and Landscaping Harvesting sea-buckthorn berries is challenging due to the dense thorns on the shrubs. A common method involves cutting entire branches, which are then frozen to facilitate berry removal. However, this approach is destructive to the plant and reduces future yields. The frozen branches are slightly defrosted during berry removal, and the berries are cleaned and stored at -22°C. Mechanical harvesting methods, such as berry-shakers developed in Estonia, are less damaging but leave up to 50% of the berries unharvested and can only be used biennially, yielding about 25% of the potential harvest. During the Cold War, Russian and East German horticulturists developed new sea-buckthorn varieties with improved nutritional value, larger berries, staggered ripening times, and branch structures that facilitate easier harvesting. In recent decades, experimental sea-buckthorn crops have been cultivated in the United States (Nevada and Arizona) and Canada (western provinces). Sea-buckthorn is also valued as a landscaping shrub, particularly for creating vandal-proof barrier hedges due to its aggressive basal shoot system. It is used in some regions to stabilize riverbanks and steep slopes. In northern climates, the plant is appreciated for its ornamental qualities, as its colorful berry clusters persist through winter. Florists also use its branches for decorative purposes. Nutrients, Potential Health Effects, and Cosmetics Sea-buckthorn berries are highly nutritious but are very acidic and astringent, making them unpleasant to consume raw unless they are bletted (exposed to frost to reduce astringency) or mixed with sweeter juices like apple or grape juice. They are also used to make pies, jams, lotions, and liquors. When pressed, sea-buckthorn juice separates into three layers: a thick orange cream on top, a middle layer rich in saturated and polyunsaturated fats, and a sediment-and-juice layer at the bottom. The top two layers are processed for cosmetic applications, such as skin creams and liniments, while the bottom layer is used for edible products. Sea-buckthorn berries are rich in antioxidants, carotenoids, vitamin E, amino acids, dietary minerals, β-sitosterol, and polyphenolic acids. The fruit's vitamin C content ranges from 114 to 1550 mg per 100 grams, with an average of 695 mg per 100 grams—approximately 12 times higher than the vitamin C content of oranges. These properties make sea-buckthorn one of the most vitamin C-enriched plant sources. The juice's freezing point of -22°C allows it to remain liquid even in sub-zero temperatures. India's Defence Research Development Organization has utilized sea-buckthorn juice to create a multi-vitamin herbal beverage for troops stationed in extremely cold environments, such as the Siachen Glacier. Sea-buckthorn is also a source of ingredients for various cosmetic products and nutritional supplements. While its nutrient and phytochemical composition suggests potential benefits for inflammatory disorders, cancer, and other diseases, no specific health benefits have been conclusively proven in humans. Traditional Medicine Sea-buckthorn has been used in traditional medicine for centuries, particularly in Asia. In China, it is used to relieve coughs, aid digestion, improve blood circulation, and alleviate pain. In Mongolia, extracts from the branches and leaves are used to treat gastrointestinal issues in both humans and animals. The bark and leaves are employed to manage diarrhea, gastrointestinal and dermatological disorders, and rheumatoid arthritis. The flowers are used as skin softeners. In Indian, Chinese, and Tibetan medicine, sea-buckthorn berries are incorporated into treatments for pulmonary, gastrointestinal, cardiac, blood, and metabolic disorders due to their hemostatic and anti-inflammatory properties. The berries are also believed to have potential anticarcinogenic activity. Fresh juice, syrups, and oils derived from the berries or seeds are used to treat colds, fever, exhaustion, stomach ulcers, cancer, and metabolic disorders. The oil, known as Chharma in some native languages, is applied to manage liver diseases, inflammation, gastrointestinal disorders (including peptic ulcers and gastritis), eczema, canker sores, wounds, burns, frostbite, psoriasis, rosacea, lupus erythematosus, and chronic dermatoses. In ophthalmology, berry extracts have been used to treat keratitis, trachoma, eyelid injuries, and conjunctivitis. Organizations The International Center for Research and Training on Seabuckthorn (ICRTS) was established in 1988 through a collaboration between the China Research and Training Center on Seabuckthorn, the Seabuckthorn Office of the Yellow River Water Commission, and the Shaanxi Seabuckthorn Development Office. ICRTS published the research journal Hippophae from 1995 to 2000, though it appears to be inactive currently. In 2005, the European Commission funded an international collaboration called EAN-Seabuck, involving the European Union, China, Russia, and New Independent States, to promote sustainable crop and product development from sea-buckthorn.
